speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the unorthodox action taken by Air Canada in firing 84 employees in New York, Cleveland and Chicago on March 29 by telephoning each employee's home between ten o'clock and eleven o'clock at night and giving the message, "You're fired. Don't report to work tomorrow morning," and in view of the fact that the only subsequent face-to-face contact these employees had-many of whom had 20 years' service-was a video-tape message from Air Canada's vice-president for the U.S. region, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT URGED TO IMPROVE SERVICE IN NEWFOUNDLAND-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that evidence given in St. John's, Newfoundland, before the Bartlett judicial inquiry into the disappearance of the trawler Cape Royal and her eight-man crew on August 9th, 1977, reveals that while there are three larger vessels, the 200-foot vessels Daring and
Alert and a 90-foot vessel Raleigh stationed at Halifax for search and rescue duties, neither of these ships were in Newfoundland waters at the time the Cape Royal vanished, and in view of the evidence that the only first-line rescue vessels in the Newfoundland region are four self-righting, 44-foot life boats that cannot go to sea in rough weather-that is, when winds are stronger than 35 or 40 miles per hour-and since the evidence reveals that coastguard radio stations in Sydney and St. Lawrence did not pass on to the Halifax search and rescue centre on August 9 distress messages received that evening, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the departments of Transport and of National Defence be censured for their neglect in failing to assign to Newfoundland at least two first-line rescue vessels of the same size and capability as those stationed in Halifax and that immediate steps be taken by the Ministers of National Defence and of Transport to have stationed in Newfoundland two such first-line rescue vessels with immediate steps taken to review and improve search and rescue capabilities in the Newfoundland and Labrador regions to ensure correction of weaknesses already revealed by evidence given before the Bartlett inquiry at St. John's.

speechtext:

My motion concerns the collapse of the dollar, in response to Monday's budget, to a 45-year low of 87.12 cents at noon today. I would add that each cent of decline in the dollar's value adds at least $300 million to the debt burden borne by Canadians.

indeed pegged at 90 cents, or confirm that he is content to allow it to float, float, float, float, and sink.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare? subsubtopic: INCREASE IN OLD AGE PENSIONS TO COMPENSATE FOR INCREASE IN CPI

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the minister not realize that the increase that will come July 1-not June 1-will be based on a period of five months back compared with three months behind that, so that the current increases in the cost of living will not be reflected in that increase; and is she not aware of the fact that promises have been made before to reconsider the formula on the cost of living index for older people? speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN OLD AGE PENSIONS TO COMPENSATE FOR INCREASE IN CPI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take another look, but I am a little disappointed. The hon. member is correct when he says it is three months' time on July 1, because the old age pensions have just been indexed. I do not understand why it was not brought to my attention by the hon. member last week.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we continue our debate on what has become known as the threepenny budget, I should like to deal with three or four separate matters which are interrelated.
I should like to deal first with the unfortunate unemployment situation in this country, to spend some time reviewing the effect of Canada's falling dollar on Canada generally, our inflation level, our unemployment level, and the deficit that this government revealed only two nights ago. I should also like to touch on the general question of inflation in Canada but, most important, I wish to tell this House and the Canadian public what we in the official opposition, what we in the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, would have wished to see in the budget that was brought in on Monday night.

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
I am sure all hon. members have noticed the references made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) with respect to unemployment. Surely two of the most startling statements he made were when he stated, "An important reason for the growth of our labour force has been the growing number of Canadian women who are working" and, secondly, "There has also been a surge of young people coming into the labour market." If we put those two comments into proper context, what the Minister of Finance, on behalf of this government, is saying is that we should not fault them for unemployment, we should fault the women of this country for unemployment because they are looking for work, and fault their children because they are also looking for work.
Can we tolerate much longer an administration that takes perhaps one of the greatest assets we have in this country, namely, our labour force, and treats it in such an utterly disdainful way?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely it is the main challenge of any government in power in any country to ensure that those who wish to work in that country become gainfully employed at the occupation of their choice.
With a budget so short of proper fiscal stimulus to ensure we will have less unemployment in this country, with a budget that virtually assures us that, if no changes are made, unemployment will not only stand at the current level of 1,040,000 but it will be higher next winter, surely there can be absolutely no confidence left in this House in an administration which, through its Minister of Finance, says "Do not blame us, blame the women of this country, and blame their children who happen to be looking for work." They happen to be looking for work, Mr. Speaker, because many families are finding it so tough to make ends meet in Canada today that more than one breadwinner must go out to work, simply to get bread on the table for those families.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Women and children first.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To deal with this question of unemployment, Mr. Speaker, we must also deal with the inter-related problems.
I would like to make a few comments concerning our falling dollar. First of all there is the great uncertainty this administration has brought into the entire picture of where it feels the dollar should be properly trading at the present time. It has been reliably estimated by those in the financial community that the handling of the falling dollar by this Minister of Finance has been inept. It has cost us three to four cents more than normally would have been expected if the dollar had been left to find its own level as far as international currencies are concerned.
Can there be much doubt left why the international world is confused as to where a dollar in Canada should trade? For example, we have a Minister of Finance who says that a floating dollar is a floating dollar, and presumably they do not intend to intervene. And yet it has been revealed that they have lost in United States dollar reserves $1.5 billion of precious reserves in defending what they said was only a floating dollar.
We know the government has borrowed $750 million in the U.S. market in an attempt to replenish some of those funds. We understand it intends to borrow further. There can be no doubt that one of the most pressing reasons why we have this budget before us today is that this administration was told it could not go back to the trough in the American money markets without showing the current fiscal 1979 figures, including the budgetary Figures, for its administration. It was a Securities and Exchange Commission requirement in the United States which helped produce the budget we are now debating in this House.
Can there be any doubt left why the international community is disturbed and concerned when we have a Minister of Finance who speaks about a floating dollar and presumably is almost indifferent as to where that dollar will settle, and we have a Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) who says that he kind of likes a 90-cent dollar, for some reason?
On the other hand when my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), put a very telling question, I thought, to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in a finance committee meeting, asking:
-would the Minister be concerned if the Canadian dollar went down to 85 or 80 cents?
Here is what a minister of the Crown, speaking on behalf of this administration, replied:
I would be concerned if the dollar went down to zero. I would be mightily concerned, because that would prove to me that nobody would want it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What a bright fellow.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not a newspaper account of what this minister said. That is the transcript from a finance committee meeting of this parliament, where a minister of the Crown said that about the only time he would really be disturbed was if our dollar went down to zero.
I know it has been jokingly stated that the government at the present time is not too disturbed about the dollar because it thinks it has 87 cents left to go, but until I heard the comment from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in that finance committee meeting, I did not realize how totally indifferent it is to the plight of our dollar.
Let us put it into perspective. It is sometimes stated that a lower valued dollar is good because it makes our exports more competitive.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Right on.

April 12, 1978

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Here is one of the loyal backbenchers who would support this government through thick and thin. In fact if they were led into hell that backbencher would say, "Let's move a little faster, if that is where you want to go, Mr. Leader."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do not interfere with the apple I am polishing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As far as that member is concerned, let me assure him that when he gets to hell, if that is where he is going, he will have so many friends he will spend most of his time greeting them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will all be Liberals.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Most of us will accept, at least temporarily, that a lower priced dollar gives a country an artificial competitive edge over other countries-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not artificial.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-in the sense it lowers its prices in relation to the currency of other nations. This consequently results in a country being more competitive, as I say, at least for a temporary period. If a nation that chooses that route of discounting its dollar does not get a hand on its own productivity, and does not control inflation in its own country, whatever temporary advantage it gains by a falling dollar is quickly eroded, and it finds that it must devalue its currency still lower to get the shot in the arm needed to continue with its export trade. This is demonstrated by the unfortunate position the United Kingdom got into when it attempted to devalue its currency two or three times, with disastrous results.
Let me come back to the Canadian situation with respect to the falling dollar. Sometimes this government gets so trapped with its policies because it picks them up second hand from something stated in the United States. It follows the Brookings Institution type of thinking almost religiously. What has happened is that somebody in the United States has said that it might be wise for the Americans to lower their dollar, or have other currencies go up in relation to the American dollar. Quickly this government said that "if it is good for the Americans, it must be good for Canada; let us have our dollar fall even faster."
When they set us on this course they totally ignored the fact that a fall in the American dollar has approximately one third the effect on the U.S. inflation level on imports that it would have in Canada. Let me be specific. Our dollar in relation to the American dollar has fallen 16 cents since the plunge began. As far as our imports are concerned, the Minister of Finance's own department clarified for us in committee that the fall will mean, built in to our inflation level, a further 4.5 per cent inflation level in Canada. That is 4.5 per cent more inflation in Canada than what we are already destined to have.
However, if the United States allowed their currency to go down in relation to other currencies by a comparable 16 cents, the total effect in the United States would be 1.5 per cent on
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
their inflation level. First, I would suggest that it is totally wrong for this government to have blindly led us into the psychology of accepting a falling dollar without realizing the consequence of inflation on Canada compared to the American position.
It is as simple as this. We in Canada have roughly 25 per cent of our total gross national product in trade. The Americans have 7 per cent. That is why it has only about a third of the effect in the United States that a falling dollar has in this country.
Let me touch the second, almost more important ingredient this government forgot when it played with a falling dollar. It forgets that in Canada, unlike in the United States, if our dollar falls, it causes various commodities in this country, domestically produced and domestically consumed, to go up in price because they are priced in accordance with the American dollar pricing. Let me be specific. Our lumber, zinc, natural resources, energy resources, cattle, and now even the fish, know about our falling dollar. Fish produce is also priced in accordance with the American dollar pricing.
What this has caused in Canada is dramatic. This is not due directly to import increases, but because so many commodities are priced in relation to an American dollar price. It is estimated that the effect of the falling dollar will cost us 3 per cent more inflation in the country. Through its inept handling of the situation, this government has triggered the falling Canadian dollar to the point where it will result in IV2 per cent additional inflation for the Canadian public to bear, a Canadian public that is already bearing an unacceptably high level of inflation as a result of the policies of this government.
Earlier today in the question period various questions were put to the Minister of Finance and certain other ministers concerning the unfortunate inflation figures that were revealed today, the fact that we had 1.1 per cent inflation in the last reported month alone, 8.8 per cent year over the year. It was also mentioned that the government's anti-inflation program as announced in October, 1975, was going to be phased out beginning this Friday. In that context, it is only fair when we are debating this budget to take a fresh look at what in fact has happened with regard to inflation in this country, certainly since this administration has been in full saddle.
In my constituency, as I am sure other members have done in their constituencies, we have maintained what we call our own grocery basket. We kept track of 15 specific grocery items just to see what in fact is the impact of inflation for the typical resident and housekeeper. My constituency is on the outskirts of Toronto. They say that Toronto is a suburb of where we live.
It is unfortunate that something is sometimes lost in statistics. When we speak about 1,045,000 out of work, I do not think it conveys the true tragedy that means for those who are out of work and looking for work. When we quote figures about 8.8 per cent inflation, or whatever figure you like, I do not think it gets through as to what that means to people who

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
are trying to put various products that they need to eat, on the table.
Let me come down to some specifics. As I say, in my constituency, we deliberately chose 15 items that are among the most usual items for the average family. I chose November, 1970, because that was when we were assured by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that he had licked inflation. Presumably we had nothing more to worry about with regard to inflation. In november, 1970, those 15 items would have cost a Canadian family $9.97. We shopped the same items last week. The cost today is $23.83.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In case some think we have selected unusual items, I hasten to add that this is a list we have maintained every six months to see what has been the progress, or lack of progress, with regard to inflation as it affects in a meaningful way the housewife trying to put groceries on the family table.
Let me give some examples of what has happened in that period since November, 1970. A 12-ounce jar of Billy Bee honey has gone from 31 cents to 83 cents. Kraft Canadian cheese slices, eight in number, weighing eight ounces, have gone from 37 cents to 93 cents. A 48-ounce tin of Mitchell apple juice has gone from 34 cents to 77 cents. Six ten-ounce cans of Coca Cola were 66 cents in 1970. Now the same number of cans sell for $1.62.
A ten-pound bag of sugar cost 96 cents then. Today it is $1.87. Two cans of Campbell's tomato soup, ten-ounce, each tin cost 24 cents in November, 1970; now they are 40 cents. Libby's pork and beans, two 19-ounce tins, 54 cents then; now $1.18. Maxwell House coffee, one-pound tin, $1.19 then; now $4.45. Sirloin steak, 99 cents a pound then; now $2.58. Special K, 15-ounce box, 56 cents in November, 1970; now $1.08. I could go on and give the whole list of those 15 items. However, the point I want to make is that those items are only typical of the effect that inflation has had on the consumer in Canada.
When this government is cornered with the facts, it loves to start looking for an escape. We used to have a minister of finance, I have forgotten how many back he was, who blamed anchovies off the coast of South America for inflation. He really turned it around two or three ways. Either they could not find them and that was a problem, or they could find them and that was a problem. In any event, when we start quoting prices, the government often blames the farmer. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, you cannot blame the farmer for the prices to which I am referring.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You cannot blame the farmer, because his costs in relation to his production have gone up even faster than the prices I have been putting on the record. The reason I wish to get on record some of the impact of inflation we are living with is that I believe the time has come when this government must be called to task.

We could go through budget after budget and, in the terms of data processing, if they had a new word processing apparatus such as are now available I would recommend that they put every budget into that word processing machine, which would save them a lot of time when they bring in another budget, because they repeat time after time the rhetoric which did not work in the preceding budget.
Now that the controls program has been in place for 30 months we should take an objective look to find out whether it has produced the result the government said it would produce. Did it bring inflation down to a lower level than might otherwise have been expected? The answer is, no. I give the figures as of February, because that is the latest date in respect of which I can make a comparison with the situation in the United States. Since then, inflation has risen by 18.3 per cent in Canada, whereas in the United States, where there are no controls, it went up by 14.3 per cent. In short, inflation here is 4 per cent worse than the level in the United States, yet we share the same continent and basically the same problems. So there is no reason to believe that anything other than the inept handling of the situation by the government has caused us this extra 4 per cent inflation as compared with the United States.
Even worse is what happened during that period. Not only was inflation in Canada 4 per cent worse, but our real growth was 3 per cent less than real growth in the United States. In the current year, the total gross national product in Canada is running approximately $6 billion below where it should be if we had simply achieved as much growth as the United States was able to achieve since October, 1975. We are talking about big money. This represents $600 of lost revenue for every Canadian taxpayer during a period of so-called government restraint, income which has been lost because of the absence of an imaginative approach by the government to ensure that our economy reaches its proper growth levels so that we can share, if you like, in the prosperity which would be the heritage of Canadians, not just for us but for our children and their children.
In short, the government does not care. It does not care what has been happening to Canadians. I understand they are polishing up a slogan for the coming election. The slogan is supposed to be "Show You Care".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Get rid of Pierre!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka says, "Show You Care; Get Rid of Pierre".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if they go to the country with that slogan I think it is only fair to remind them that they have not cared much about Canada or the Canadian people. All that possibility of real growth has been lost by the government. If we were able to get the Canadian work force back to work there would be no deficit-there would not be the $10.9 billion deficit which the Minister of Finance disclosed Monday night.
April 12, 1978

That deficit he is talking about represents $500 for every man, woman and child in Canada. That is the extent to which the government has gone into the hole.
I have compared inflation and real growth in Canada with that in the United States. I could go on and make comparisons with the situation in other industrialized nations. Perhaps it would be only fair for me to say that, compared with the countries of the OECD, we have the highest unemployment level of any, our inflation level is running higher than average inflation in those countries, our real growth is below that in any of those countries, our current account trade deficit, worsened by such things as our imbalanced tourist account, is higher than that in any of the OECD countries. And all this results in our being the only industrialized nation which has run a current account deficit consistently for the past four years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But they are keeping cool.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, they are keeping cool, as my hon. friend says. They are indifferent. They do not care. They care about one thing. They care about their political hides.
Consider the decade which has passed, one which began after the first hundred years of Confederation, at a time when we had reached one of the highest peaks of prosperity ever reached by any country in the world. As that decade began, the philosophy guiding this administration was one of government expediency. That was the order of the day. Economic realities came second.
Let me go back to the subject of the Anti-Inflation Board. The Board was set up in October, 1975, when we were told that along with this program the government would introduce other measures of financial restraint

which it did not. At that time we were promised additional monetary restraint. Once again we were deceived.
They said there would be a general regulation of the economy-which there wasn't-plus the AIB program. They were to get us down to an 8 per cent level of inflation the first year, to a 6 per cent level the next year, and to 4 per cent in the year which is now current. But we find, Mr. Speaker, that today we are at about the same estimated level of inflation we were told we would be seeing at the end of the first year. One thing the government has excelled in, Mr. Speaker, is the ability to create inflation in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When I say they know how to create inflation in this country I think every member of this House is under an obligation to remind the Canadian public that inflation is literally manufactured by this government by the excess printing of money in relation to the real growth of our economy. Last year, for example, with a real growth of 2.6 per cent, is it any wonder that we ended up with 9.5 per cent inflation? Consider this: they printed 12 per cent more money last year. Less 2.6 per cent, the difference is almost exactly the 9.5 per
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
cent inflation which plagued this nation as of December, 1977. But that is not only the impact of the controls program.
The fact is that the approach of the government has been counter-productive. That approach has killed business initiative. It has contributed to the unemployment we are living with, and let me give figures. In March, 1975, which was the March before the controls program was imposed, there were 739,000 Canadians out of work. On a non-adjusted basis that was 7.6 per cent of the work force. On an adjusted basis it was 6.8 per cent of the work force. This March unemployment is up 300,000 compared to what it was in March, 1975. There are 1,045,000 out of work today compared with 739,000 prior to the beginning of the controls program. Expressed on an adjusted basis there is now 8.6 per cent of the work force out of work compared with the 6.8 per cent to which I referred as of March, 1975.
I think the Canadian public is aware of the inadequacies. It is aware that there must be a better way to get the Canadian economy achieving the potential which most feel-and certainly that includes members of this party-can be achieved in Canada.
In the few moments I have available I would like to touch on what this party would have liked to have seen, or would have put into the budget Monday night if we had been given that opportunity. There are three essential things which must be accomplished if we are to reach a new prosperity. First, we must once again restore consumer confidence. We must take the consumer willing to buy more because, the more he buys, the more our factories will produce, the more people they will employ, and the more prosperity there will be for all. If we had been writing a budget on Monday night, we would have put into it stimulative fiscal measures in order to ensure that the consumer would start to get back his confidence and would start to do the buying which is so sorely needed in the country.
Second, if we had had the opportunity, we would have proposed certain infrastructure investments which are sorely needed to aid fishermen on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, to aid those who handle grain in the Canadian west, to aid commuters in Toronto and other urban areas of Canada, and to help with sewage treatment plants in areas such as Montreal which need that kind of help.
The third thing we would have suggested is that it is time to put some meaningful productivity incentives into our system so that people at work benches, in factories, or wherever they produce, will produce still more to ensure that our competitiveness is restored. To that end we would have suggested on Monday night that there should be personal income tax cuts. Consumers need a break, and by reducing the tax burden on Canadians, in our view the economy would be set firmly on the path to recovery.
I know people often ask how there can be a tax cut without running up the deficit. The unique thing is that both problems can be solved at the same time. If a tax cut is stimulative, it will produce the gross national wealth which is needed to
4436

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
increase tax revenues, and the net effect is a deficit which is smaller that it would have been if the situation had been allowed to continue, and it is in a lethargic state now. That proposal was not just pulled out of the air. Before we enunciated our program with respect to a minimum $2 billion tax cut, we asked economic consultants to program their computers in order to tell us what a $2 billion personal income tax cut would do for Canada.
Two computer programs came back. They both suggested the same results. I would like to put on the record the net effect of such a measure. We were told that the rise in the level of gross national product would be 3.9 times the initial tax reduction. In relation to a $2 billion permanent personal tax cut, if such were implemented in 1978, the gross national product in 1980 would be $7.5 billion to $8 billion higher than it would be without the tax cut. That is why we would have announced a tax cut if we had brought down a budget on Monday night. The economy needs it. The economy needs that type of stimulant to get us producing, to bring our unemployment down and, at the same time, to bring our inflation level down.
Let me be more specific. As consumer spending accounts for more than 60 per cent of our national output, sustained weakness in this sector aborts any economic recovery. Revived consumer spending can lead the way to reduced unemployment, higher disposal incomes, and that most desirable of all things, real growth.
Increased consumer spending would allow Canadian industry to produce more goods. More production means more jobs. As industry produces more, business investment increases, thus creating more jobs. If we had had the opportunity to write that budget, we would have proposed personal income tax cuts generally, but we believe they should be oriented to help where it counts, that is, to put more spending money into the pocket of the consumer. For many Canadians the tax cut we propose would be $300, not on a temporary basis but on a permanent basis, so that people can count on more money in the coming weeks, months, and years ahead. To be most meaningful we believe that a tax should be oriented to low and middle income Canadians, who are the greatest spenders or consumers because they need every nickel they can get to make ends meet.
It is very important that a tax cut be permanent. When the government instituted its $100 tax cut, $50 in January of this year and another $50 in February of this year, it missed the point. In allowing that tax cut the government lost revenue totalling $700 million. The government said that tax cut would have a stimulative effect, but as far as I know very few wage earners in Canada even know their taxes were ever cut.
In fact most people are left with the impression that somehow their taxes went up $50 in March, and they do not understand why. I believe that fiscal measure was perhaps one of the most stupid things ever done by a department of finance. If the government wanted to produce the maximum benefit from a tax cut, that was not the way to do it. We say a tax cut must be on a permanent basis so that Canadians can

count on it and so that, if they want to buy something, they know what their take home pay will be for the next 12 months. Canadians do not want gimmicks of the kind the government introduced in January and February.
We have in this budget a proposal to institute a 3 per cent provincial sales tax reduction. Here again the government has what could be a good idea, but from an administrative standpoint the effects of this proposal will be minimal. The government says provincial sales taxes should be cut for only six months, and possibly nine months in certain provinces. That would tend to cause people, if they are going to buy as a result of this tax concession, to telescope their buying into the period of the tax concession, which would result in a bigger problem in getting factories to produce in the winter months ahead. That is the time when jobs are needed, because traditionally unemployment in this country increases in the winter months over its level during the summer months.
Again, by putting it on a temporary basis, somehow or other they do not give any certainty to the would-be buyer or consumer in this country. Again they clouded the issue, and it may be that while it will cost them $800 million in loss of revenue, they will get a minimum benefit from their approach as compared with the benefit they could have had if they had taken the $700 million which they spent in January and February, and the $800 million they are now proposing to spend, and lumped them together with a permanent personal income tax reduction of $2 billion plus which we are suggesting.
I could go on to demonstrate why those half measures do not work so far as fiscal policy is concerned. I have suggested that our approach would tend to lower inflation, but I want to stress that it is conditional upon having a proper cutback in government spending. We believe that the government, in budget after budget, has talked about restraint, but we do not think it is sincere. In fact, it is rather startling to find in the budget which is now before us an admission, a confession, if you like, by the Minister of Finance that the government has made mistakes in the past concerning spending.
At the beginning of his budget speech the minister stated:
It is now clear that many of our current difficulties have their roots in the period of extraordinary growth Canada experienced between the mid-1960's and the mid-1970's.
He went on to say:
Governments increased their spending too quickly. The money supply was increased too fast.
Surely the Minister of Finance does not need to be told who was in power when that mistake was made. To come in now on April 10 and say it was a mistake, and to create the impression somehow that his predecessor or he himself should not be blamed, is absolutely ludicrous.
If we had had the opportunity to bring in the budget on Monday night, we would have been proposing a three-year program to cut $2 billion plus from federal spending. We feel that this can be done without reducing transfer payments to
April 12, 1978

Canadians, without cutting back on federal capital expenditures, and without disrupting essential services in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not truly remarkable that the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), who is freshly out of the absolute shambles in his Post Office portfolio, now asks me "how"? For anybody who is a member of an administration which has allowed the Post Office Department, which was profitable in 1970-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Come on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -to run into a position where it now has a deficit of $500 million to $600 million, in spite of repeated postage rate increases, to ask that shows lack of depth.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It also shows the lack of control which the government has of financing and of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go steam open some letters, J.-J.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go lick a stamp.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hear the former postmaster general say he does not agree with my figures. I would be very pleased to take him down and show him the national financing figures and show him, year by year, where the deficit has occurred and how the expenses have risen much faster than the revenues. I think that even he, if I spend enough time, will understand exactly what I mean.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would not count on that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be a waste of time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Even he would understand how the Post Office got into trouble.
I have said that if we had had the opportunity to present a budget on Monday night, we would have proposed trimmings in federal spending which would have resulted in the federal spending being reduced by $2 billion within a three-year period. First of all let us note that operating costs account for more than 32 per cent of government spending, and it is in the area of operating costs that the government has allowed a growth of 56 per cent in the last three years. The government has allowed those costs to jump by 56 per cent during a period when it has implored the private sector to be more restrained in its own spending. If operating costs had increased only at the rate that workers' wages were allowed to increase during the time when the anti-inflation program was in effect, federal spending today would be $3.3 billion lower than at present.
I heard one of the faithful backbenchers on the government side ask where we are going to get these savings. My leader is on record concerning certain areas where we intend to make savings when we have the opportunity to write a budget. The hon. member is asking for details. We believe that a program
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
could have been instituted on Monday night providing for a public service hiring freeze. That is the first thing we would have done.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have had one for three years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The former postmaster general says they have had a hiring freeze. Surely even he could count up to 25,000, which is the number of extra employees his Post Office has hired since the 1970 period to which I have referred. When they talk about a public service freeze, what they mean is that the number of public servants has increased less quickly than it did the year before. What we are saying is that the number should not go up at all, and that there should be no replacement of the attrition that is normal in any public service. For example, there would be no replacement of the people who retire or of the people who choose to leave.
In short, over a one-year period there are approximately 20,000 employees who, for one reason or another, leave the Public Service. We simply propose that those positions not be filled. That would result, over a three-year period, in a reduction of 50,000 to 60,000 employees at the federal government level. That is what we mean by a freeze.
I think I should make clear that it would not be our intention to make any reductions in our military personnel, in our prison guards, or in our Mounties.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is already half of all the government employees.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not including those fields, the figures I have given are figures which the Minister of Finance could have mentioned in his budget on Monday night had he had the courage to be a responsible minister rather than the part-time minister he has been.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We would also propose that the personnel supports which go with the Public Service also be reduced. That is another cost saving which we would have proposed on Monday night. For example, it means there would be lower accommodation and equipment charges, lower transportation and communication expenditures. One must recall that taxi cab fares in Ottawa run up by the government are over $1 million a year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Additional reductions in spending can be achieved through sharply reduced advertising and consulting expenditures. If we are given an opportunity by the Canadian public to take over the reins of government in this country, there will be a great many Liberal advertising hacks, friends, and consultants who will lose their contracts pretty fast.
Significant savings can be made from the $50 million spending spree this government is on by implementing the concept of having sunset laws instituted, with zero based budgeting.
80033-68V4

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
Basically that means, rather than accepting last year's spending figures without question, we would propose that every new spending estimate be assessed as to why it is needed in the coming year. Unless it can be justified and shown to have significant value for the Canadian public, we would say it should be dropped and the saving should be passed back to the Canadian public.
The sunset law concept works the same way. No law should be regarded as so sacred that it cannot be reviewed. It is as natural to discontinue programs as it is to create them. Surely the government of the day should be assessing constantly the impact of the programs available, thus discerning if they are an advantage or a disadvantage, if they should be continued or dropped. That is what my party would have included Monday night, if we had had the opportunity of presenting the budget.
Many of the 400 Crown corporations were created under this administration. We believe some of them can be dismantled, integrated within departments, or sold to the private sector. Non-budgetary borrowings of Crown corporations must be curtailed, especially where the interest rate does not reflect market conditions.
The economic stimulus given by the tax cut, to which I referred coupled with reductions in federal spending, would combine to hold the budgetary deficit steady at first, and then to reduce it. New consumer spending would increase. Incidentally, it would increase sales tax revenue, excise tax revenue, and customs duty revenue. The newly created jobs would produce new taxpayers. As the business climate because more healty in response to increased consumer demands, there would be more revenues from federal corporation taxes. In addition to the savings of the expenditure reductions which I have outlined, federal spending on unemployment benefits would also drop the more we were able to get Canadians back to work in gainful jobs.
Perhaps I could simply sum up by saying: if we had the opportunity of presenting the budget Monday night, we would have made federal spending restraint a way of life in Ottawa.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In our minds, the three-year program to which I have referred would be just the start. It would be the start of a comprehensive effort to reduce the federal presence in our economy, to reduce the dead hand of government which is stifling individual initiative and which is stifling people from achieving Canada's dream that has disappeared so much under this government.
We have referred to the rather small provincial sales tax reduction. There is room to reduce the federal manufacturing tax as well. For example, that tax is very inflationary, because at its 12 per cent level it goes on to the manufacturing level, simply to be magnified as the goods eventually go through to the consumer. When the wholesaler takes his add-on, when the retailer takes his add-on, and the province adds its provincial sales tax to that 12 per cent, in short it means that a 12 per cent tax at the federal government level results in a 28 per cent higher price for most Canadian consumers. There is room to

remove and reduce that type of tax to ensure that it is not as regressive as it is at the present time. That is our reason for proposing to reduce it. By reducing federal tax, it would be stimulative but non-inflationary, as far as the economy is concerned.
There is room for more imaginative corporate tax measures than the government has proposed. In that category, it is important that tax measures designed to encourage productivity within corporations should have a hooker on them to ensure those corporations respond in a manner which the government of the day feels is advantageous to Canadians. This has been advanced repeatedly in the House by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees). Certainly the government is aware of it. Because he was a former minister of industry, trade and commerce, the hon. member knows how important it is to design a package of tax stimulants to receive the impact and the benefit we are looking for, and not take anything for granted.
I should like to touch upon a more meaningful manner of implementing incentives to encourage research and development. We are pleased the government went part of the way on Monday night to encourage research and development, but we feel much more can be done. There is room to allow for inflatioft in corporate accounting before paying taxation. This is long overdue. There should be meaningful ways to get Canadians investing, especially in Canadian small business. On Monday night we would have introduced some concrete measures to accomplish that end.
Perhaps what is most missing in the government's approach is a longer range perspective. On Monday night the Minister of Finance should have given the nation a five-year performance projection. Why must we always be dealing in fiscal and monetary positions over the next few months, without realizing that it is the two-year, three-year, and five-year positions which should be concentrated on, to ensure that today's severe problems will not be worse in three to five years down the road? That is why, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is most unfortunate that we do not have the five-year targets written into the budgetary papers presented Monday night. Let the country know the real growth targets of the government. What are the employment targets, the inflation levels? What does the government foresee in its own expenditure plans in the next five-year period?
Every industrialized nation is starting to set up such plans. Presumably this government would do it if it knew what to show over the next five years in those forecasts. The hard fact is that it literally does not know what to do tomorrow to help the Canadian economy, let alone what should be done five years down the road. In that context, Mr. Speaker, I would like to move:
That all the words after the word "That" be struck out and the following substituted therefor: "-in the opinion of this House the failure of the budget to curtail federal spending constitutes an admission by the government that it has lost control of the economy, and the temporary sales tax cut, to end before next winter, will not reduce unemployment and inflation, stimulate real growth,
April 12, 1978

reduce the budgetary deficit or stabilize the dollar, as would a minimum S2 billion permanent tax cut for Canadians."
My motion is seconded by my colleague, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has been my pleasure, Mr. Speaker, over the years to follow the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), and I must confess that at times I have had a twinge of conscience about doing so because it has offered me the opportunity of rebuttal and to take exception to some of his remarks, without giving him the same opportunity when I speak. I must admit, however, that I have no qualms today after listening to the hon. member for an hour and a half in his oration. As erudite and wise as the hon. member is, and as interesting as the things he says may be, since we are on live television I suspect it is a Conservative plot to make sure that the NDP do not have an audience.
It was my original intention to deal with the government's budget in my remarks; however, I think I must comment on some of the matters raised by the hon. member for York-Simcoe since they are being put forward as alternatives to the government's proposals.
In this day and age it is fashionable to talk about cutting back on government expenditures and such things. The first issue I would like to raise, and I think it is important, is the one and a half million people unemployed, most of whom are young men and women. Most of these young men and women have had some expectation of finding jobs for which they have been trained. But the private sector is not hiring at all. There are virtually no opportunities for our young men and women to find employment. Yet the proposal put forward by the Conservative party through the hon. member for York-Simcoe is that we put a freeze on public service hiring.
Let us look at the ramifications of such a proposal. What it means is that there is not going to be an opportunity at all for young people who are coming out of our school system. Is that what we want? We are not going to let them starve, so will unemployment insurance, Opportunities for Youth, or some similar organization make work projects for them? It sounds great when they say, "Freeze hiring in the Public Service," but translate that into what it means to the people coming into the labour market.
The government's budget is a prescription for disaster, but the kinds of suggestions that we are getting from the Conservative party are a double subscription to total disaster and are completely thoughtless. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe and everyone in this House knows, the mood of the public is against public expenditures. But standing up to this mood and saying, "Look, there are limits to public expenditures, we agree that there has to be efficiency in the public sector," is not enough. Instead, they pander to the worst kind of prejudice regarding this kind of situation and say, "We are going to freeze all hiring in the public sector." Think about what that really means.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, to have to disrupt my talk on the budget in order to deal with this, but I think it has to be dealt
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
with because, again, it is this pandering to fears that exist in our society that is worrisome, and it should not happen. We talk about a permanent tax cut of $2 billion. That sounds great, but what happens if you have a tax cut of $2 billion? If you lock a government into saying, "We will not raise taxes regardless of what happens to the cost of living", it means the government's revenues are locked in. If I thought for one moment that the prescription of the Conservative party, the Liberal party or any party in the western world really had an answer to inflation-some of us have better answers than others-that would be fine. However, we all know that in the western world inflation is a very troublesome issue and nobody has a total answer.
If you have an adjustment because of indexing and you say there is not going to be a raise in taxes, what happens? The cost of living goes up; old age pensioners have to be told the government revenue is not there, so we cut back the old age pension; there is no money to give to the hospitals, so we will throw the patients out; we cannot deal with medicare; we cannot deal with people who need social services-throw it out; and we cut back on veterans' pensions. It sounds great when they say permanent tax cuts, but I would not like to have a permanent tax cut because it is dishonest. It cannot be done. If it is done, it is done at the expense of those people who look to the government to provide them with some of the services they are entitled to expect because of their own contributions to society. This is a great danger.
We all know there is somewhat of a right wing swing in the country and, therefore, there are certain kinds of prejudices. Instead of dealing with some of the prejudices and saying, "Look, while there is some truth, there is always some truth to these things, let us look at the whole picture", we have a situation where the Conservative party goes out and irresponsibly inflames these prejudices. It is irresponsible for that party to do such a thing, particularly when they are standing here today trying to criticize the government on the measures in the budget. There was hardly a word of criticism about the specifics of the budget.
For an hour and one-half I listened very carefully to the hon. member for York Simcoe, and he had hardly anything to say about the proposals in the budget. Although this is supposed to be the budget debate, he scarcely dealt with any of those issues. Particularly, he did not deal with the issue we thought he would have welcomed, the cutback in the sales tax at the provincial level in conjunction with the provincial governments. After all, this was a Tory idea that the Liberals stole. It is rather rude when you deny your paternity. I think you can make a great case out of it. It is quite obvious why the Conservative party had to deal with the other measures-they did not want to acknowledge the Liberal party was becoming as right-wing as they are.
Looking at the budget there can be no doubt that we are going into an election. In his opening remarks the Minister of

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
Finance (Mr. Chretien), when he was being very sanctimonious, said:
Many of the suggestions made to me for this budget would be popular politically but unwise economically. I will not follow such suggestions. I believe this is time for Canada to face our problems critically and realistically.
I wish he had done that. I would have applauded him myself. He did not do it, however, but did just the opposite. He took a whole bunch of short-term, short-sighted ideas, put them into a package that he thought would have the maximum appeal for an election, and brought that forward as a budget. I want to examine each of those proposals he has put before us, Mr. Speaker, and that he has asked us to consider as some sort of answer to the deep problems facing the country.
When I first read the budget I had doubts about the authorship. I suspected that, rather than being written by officials in the Department of Finance, it had the hallmarks of the fine hand of Keith Davey and "Boots" Coutts. It was written in the marble halls of the Senate and the Prime Minister's office. It was a political document designed for political purposes. I think there should be resentment that, facing the kind of problems we face in this country, the government would stoop so low as to try to put this piece of cosmetics before us as a budget and as a way of suggesting it is going to do the job.
I suspect there would have been a great deal more criticism with a different Minister of Finance. Most people like and admire the minister. He looks very honest, and sometimes even manages to be one of the few on that side of the House who look somewhat humble.
On budget night we had a picture of self flagellation by the minister in admitting that the government in the past might not have done everything it should have done, but claiming they are now very contrite and humble and are asking forgiveness. We even had some pictures in the newspapers showing the minister as a human being with his lovely family. It was all part of an attempt to say that "what is past, is past, and now we are on the right road." I am sorry that the respect most of us have for the minister cannot be translated into any kind of respect for the budget he has put before us.
The old villains have been trotted out. It is the fault of everybody except "us chickens on the government side." There is a nice phrase where the minister said the money supply was increased too fast. I think he has been listening to too many of the speeches of the hon. member for York-Simcoe and has picked up his wisdom there. Sometimes it is hard to know them apart without a road map.
I am glad to see the hon. member for York-Simcoe in the House. I want to say something in connection with a remark he made during his intervention when he talked about the money supply and, in ominous terms, pointed out that the growth of the money supply was around 12 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Real growth, 2.6 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A real growth of 2.6 per cent, and that the rate of inflation was the difference between 2.6 per cent and

the money supply. What he was saying was that if the money supply had not been increased to 12 per cent we would not have had any inflation-that the entire inflation came about because the money supply was increased. That was certainly the impression he meant to leave.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is what he said.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I ask the hon. member for York-Simcoe, as a reasonable man, is it not possible that if prices go up by 12 per cent, you have to increase the money supply by 12 per cent in order to get identical circulation in a society?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that not a reasonable assumption? Why would you assume, if you saw an ostrich with its head in the sand, that what was poking out was its face?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You missed the whole point.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry. I shall have to take a private lesson on this because that is certainly the impression I got- that if only you could control the money supply that would be the end of inflation. This simple little manoeuvre does not occur to that stupid government over there. I am not saying the government has the greatest brain or greatest genius in the world, but if it were that simple the problem would have been solved a long time ago. After all, the opposition must have something to say. The minister did not stop with the money supply but pointed out the other people involved-too many young people coming on the labour market, too many women coming on the labour market, and too much appropriation in Canada. All these things are apparently the fault of the economy.
I am not prepared to say that everything that goes wrong is the government's fault, but a lot of it is. We know the world is facing serious economic problems, not just Canada, and not just the United States. I am not going to make the kind of comparison made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, who pointed out that the rate of inflation in Canada over an 18-month period was 16 per cent, while it was only 14 per cent in the United States, and that therefore the AIB program is a failure.
The government is to blame for this. It has been wrong in virtually every one of its forecasts. It has learned nothing from the past, and does not seem to be willing to learn from the experience it is presently going through. It still pursues the same course.
In the election I hope the government or those others here do not win a majority, both for the sake of the country and of my own party. If they do, we will have a perpetuation of the disastrous social and economic policies we have seen over the years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did you chicken out last time?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sure they could teach us. They could teach us to be more successful as a political party, but I doubt
April 12, 1978

whether they could teach us to be more honest, more straightforward, or have better ideas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When you are not the winner, success is not everything.
I would like to look at some of the specifics in the budget just to show how effective some of the measures will be. The first one is research and development, and we will start with motherhood as it is always a good place to start. Everyone is in favour of research and development. After all, who can be opposed to extra grants and special benefits to encourage research and development? We are all in favour of it.
What has been the experience in Canada? Canada, over the years, has had one of the most generous policies of research and development of any country. Over the years we have allocated sums of money in the budget for research and development. It was one of the few items in federal budgets which was never spent because it was never picked up. It will not be picked up this time either. The problem is quite clear. You will get some research and development, and to the extent that it will create some jobs for Canadian scientists I am happy for that and I will not knock that, but to expect that there will be any kind of significant improvement in research and development is nonsense.
The reason research and development are not carried out in Canada is not because we have not tried to give encouragement; it is because most of our firms which are in a position to do this are foreign owned. And because of this they will not get into research and development in Canada, and they have not done any. Even where they have carried out research and development in Canada, we still do not benefit. We might get a few jobs for engineers and scientists, but the real benefits from research and development come with the creation of the mass production jobs. When the technology is applied to the plant, it will go back to the head office. There is no provision which says that technology must stay here.
There are fewer patents registered in Canada than anywhere else in the world. Even if something is invented in Canada and we pay for it through tax dollars, we do not receive the benefits from that sort of thing. Research and development are very valuable. Who will argue against research and development? But it is not true that we have done anything effective in that area, and we cannot do anything effective in that area until the government develops an industrial strategy which deals with the question of foreign ownership.
With respect to energy development incentives, it is remarkable that we are living in an age where, in less than 100 years, we have virtually consumed all the fossil energy which has taken nature billions of years to create. In one generation we have consumed it. Where do the incentives go for that small dwindling resource that is still left of fossil fuels? How much is left? No matter what we do or how we reduce our consumption, do we have more than 50 years or 100 years left? Is that
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
where the incentives should go to reduce it even further than it is at the moment? My friend, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) says, "Let it stay there, it will not go bad". It has been there a long time.
I think we need to give incentives in the field of energy. If we are going to do that, surely it should be in the area of renewable energy. There are lots of areas in which incentives are required. There are lots of jobs which could be created in the area of nuclear energy, tidal power, and solar energy, and work could be done in those areas. But we do not do that. Instead, incentives are given to the oil companies which really do not need it all that badly. If in fact it turns out these companies become very profitable, the province of Alberta will take it away from them, and the province of Saskatchewan as well, to a smaller degree; Saskatchewan is a little more sensitive. Those are two of the great items in the budget.
Let me demonstrate, Mr. Speaker, the difference and the attitude which our party would take on a certain item as compared to what the government has proposed. I am speaking particularly of railway investment. We know, and I think all of us acknowledge, that rail beds must be improved, the rolling stock must be improved. In an era of tight energy, rail transportation is an important development which we should be looking at, especially passenger services.
Our party proposes that one of the fastest and most useful ways to invest in the future is by putting people to work fixing up roadbeds, and getting the work done on the roadbeds now while the unemployment level is high. This is in preference to paying them unemployment insurance. We have suggested this before as a government program. I am not talking about doing it out of current taxation. The money could be borrowed, special bonds could be issued; after all, it is a capital investment. It would solve two problems. It would give us the type of infrastructure we need for the future, and it would correct this horror of unemployment of the present. But no, the government will not touch it. However, it has to deal with it in some way. It does this by giving the railroads a special concession of 6 per cent depreciation allowance, an extra allowance, if they will make some of these improvements.
What is the difference? If it is done on a national basis, it is done for the national interest. If it is done on a business basis through depreciation allowances, for example the CPR and the CNR later on, because they say they will operate just like the CPR-Gresham's law the bad drives out the good, it is not the good that reforms the bad-when will they do it? They will do it when it suits their corporate interest, when it suits their balance sheets, not when it suits the national interest. I am not critical of the way the CPR is doing it; this is the way the world is. It is the government which must be condemned.
In effect the government is saying if companies feel like going along with improvements when it suits their interests, then it could be done. We in this party think it is of critical importance to this country that these programs should be commenced immediately. That is an example of the difference in policies. Even if you take an idea which has some merit, by the time the government gets through twisting and distorting it

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
and trying to find some way to make it fit into its precious free enterprise system, there is not much left of it for the nation.
Let us go on to another matter, that of the retail sales tax. I think this is not a bad measure, either as a temporary or a long-term measure. I want to say there is some benefit to this. If one is to give a fast stimulus to the economy, the most effective way to give that stimulus is to cut the retail sales tax. What is the consequence? Six months, nine months, depending on which option is taken. In the six months now when employment generally is a little better than average, the stimulus will occur.
This stimulus will work, but not to the extent the government thinks. This six-months period will end just before the winter. People will have made their large purchases. There will be ads in the last month saying "Quickly, Quickly, Quickly; Buy, Buy, Buy Now. Do Not Wait, The Tax Is Going Back On". Instead of the seven years of the pharaohs, the seven good years or the seven lean years, we will have six good months, and then six disastrous months in the middle of the winter when we need employment the most. That is irresponsible. That is short-term, and it is designed for no other reason than to make the government look better in the middle of an election period. I think it is wrong, and it must be said that the budget should not be used for this purpose.
I understand, to the credit of the minister, that he did not want a budget. That is the rumour. I do not know; I have not asked him. He has not volunteered the information. But I assume he did not want the budget because he knew the kind of budget for which he would have to be responsible. I guess the politicians and the boys in the finance department could have told him that there is not much that you can do with short-term stuff; longer term measures have to be undertaken if they are to succeed. But my good friend in the other place, Senator Davey, probably said, "We have to have a budget. We may not gain any points from this budget because it will be a little transparent, people will see through it, but if you go into an election and the Tories are screaming at you "How dare you go into an election without a budget" then it might cost us some votes. If you break even on the budget, you have done well.
They certainly are not going to win any kudos from this budget, but they may break even. People will say there is a lot of truth in what you say, and criticism is valid. They will say they can get a car for a couple of hundred dollars less. A break is a break. People are not ungrateful.
The budget was designed, and I greet this with some approval, to stimulate consumption. That is one of the chief problems as far as unemployment is concerned. Our society is suffering from an inadequacy of consumption. Our subamendment will try to deal with that in a somewhat better way than the amendment.
We have been suffering from under consumption. Consumption has to be stimulated. We do not object to the kind of stimulus such as the sales tax measure, but to the short-term

nature of it and the problems it will create. However, the problems will be created after the election. If they have a majority, they do not need to worry about it for four years.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: God help us!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As my friend says, God help us! They are trying to stimulate the economy, trying to create consumer demand. Then they turn around and find here is another groups of disaffected people whom they think they can buy off very cheaply. The way to buy them off is to sweeten the provisions of the Registered Retirement Savings Plans. After all, it is mostly the rich who use them, not the poor.
By sweetening the benefits, they increase the amount of savings. On the left hand, they are trying to encourage consumption by cutting taxes. They do not know their left hand from their right. With their right hand, they are encouraging savings. What kind of a policy is that, with one offsetting the other? If the minister did not understand it or was not aware of the problem, you could say it was pure stupidity. It was not that, because the minister understands. For six months he has been going around the country, and he made reference to it in the question period today, saying that we in this country are saving too much money, that we should be spending the money, not saving it.
Saving is a private virtue, but if everybody starts to save, it becomes a public disaster. That created the depression in the thirties to some extent. We may in fact be saving ourselves into a depression right now. One reason we cannot recover as quickly as we could is because the level of savings is just too high.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister applauds. I thank him for that. I know he understands. However, why perpetuate programs like the Registered Retirement Savings Program, and then sweeten it to encourage more savings at a time when the problem is consumption? This is the difficulty. How can anyone be asked to look at this budget with credibility and without suspicion, seeing these two contradictory items side by side? This is what makes the whole thing so difficult.
I want to conclude, not because there is not a great deal more to say, but I am not in the fortunate position of the spokesman for the official opposition in having unlimited time.
I do not have unlimited time. I also have a subamendment that I want to move.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have another ten minutes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My unofficial leader, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just checked the clock. He tells me I have another ten minutes. Now I want to talk about what we need to do.
We need to start thinking about what is happening to our society. We must stop kidding ourselves. The government kids us by saying "everything is all right, it is the money supply,
April 12, 1978

there are too many young people, too many people are getting into bed with each other and having too many children and we have to do something about that." They say that is creating all the problems. The opposition state we have too many public servants, we have to get rid of the public servants and we have to freeze taxes, without really thinking out the consequences about what they are saying. I know it is a difficult time we live in, difficult in the sense that a lot of the old rules just do not apply.
I am supporting a tax cut in my subamendment. A tax cut will do some good, particularly if it is as suggested in our subamendment, at the very lowest end of the income scale, and if it is coupled with a tax credit so that those who do not have the income to pay tax will get some benefit and do some spending.
We, in effect, have two societies side by side. Every time you cut the tax of one, you increase their savings. They have reached that kind of satiation point. They do not need things that badly. The other group needs things very badly, but does not have the money.
What we are seeing in our society is the old, old problem, except now it has become an economic rather than a social problem. It is a problem of income distribution. Those who have it do not need to spend, and those who would spend and get the economy rolling again do not have it. We need something similar to an internal Marshall Plan. We see no signs of it in anything the government proposes.
In fairness to the government, I must say one of the reasons I like the sales tax proposal, in contrast to some of the other proposals, is that it has a leveller effect. It tends to help people at the lowest end of the income scale as much as it helps the others. Of the options, that is the preferred one.
We need to have income redistribution in some way. That does not mean more incentives for people with money. We have to be prepared to tax those who have money, for their own sake. This is the great irony of our times. People do not want to pay taxes to help the unemployed. They do not want their money to go to some of the depressed areas of Canada. But it must go whether they like it or not, unless they are prepared to see people starving in the streets.
Those who are working complain about the taxes they are paying. They are paying unemployment insurance and other things. With better income redistribution, the consequence would be to put more people back to work. A lot of what they are now paying for would not be necessary. Even though taxes might seem to be a little higher, Canadians would be infinitely better off than now. The work would be shared. More people would be happy. The burden of maintaining society would be borne by everyone instead of a few.
There is no escape from this dilemma in a modern society. Either everyone works and everyone carries some of the burden, or those who are working carry the burden for those who are not. That is the choice. It is not a matter of saying "I am going to work, and the hell with the other guy." Fortunate-
The Budget-Mr. C. A. Gauthier ly our society has gone past that stage. We are much too civilized and decent to do that sort of thing.
When taxes were cut previously, it turned out to be a very powerful stimulus. Now, depending on whose taxes are cut, it can either be a stimulus or it can result in more savings. Much of the tax cuts of the past have not gone into consumption, but into savings. This has compounded the problem. For tax cuts to be effective, they must take place in areas where the benefits or the returns for those tax cuts are going to be spent. That is what must be done if you want to stimulate the economy and stimulate consumer purchasing power.
In many ways what I am saying is that income redistribution is no longer just a question of morality. It is no longer what the socialist believes in, that income redistribution is good, that one person should not be very rich while another is very poor. It is more than just morality more than just political ideology. Either it will be done or our society will not survive. It is an economic necessity. Therefore, when we look at these measures, we must look at them with great care to ensure that the tax cuts do not go into those areas which will compound the problem but go to those areas which will improve the situation.
Therefore, in the light of what I have said, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre:
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House calls for such an income tax cut to be directed mainly to those in the lower income brackets, including the provision of tax credits to those who are below the exemption levels, to stimulate production and provide jobs for unemployed Canadians."
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every time I have had the opportunity of commenting on a budget, I always did take time to think of the minister who had introduced it. I have witnessed a succession of finance ministers in this House during nearly 16 years and I have noticed that they never lasted long in this office.
