This is why I am more inclined to sympathize with these men who have at least the courage to face up to a department which is perhaps fatal for any minister, since most of them lose their hides and those who do not succumb are disabled or sent to rest in the Senate, which is not a better fate. I do not wish that to happen to the present minister who is still young but I simply want to tell him before starting my remarks that I sympathize with him because he has been compelled by circumstances to present this budget. Some weeks ago people were wondering if a budget was actually going to be presented and the government did not seem to have the capacity or the will to do so. There was a change of mind every week on the subject and finally we end up with a semblance of a budget.
While reading over the financial statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) I acknowledge with him that we are living in very troubled times and that our problems are as

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. C. A. Gauthier complex as they are difficult. With an unprecedented unemployment level that is a total of 1,045,000 workers seeking jobs and collecting benefits as long as they are eligible, not to mention all those who cannot draw any unemployment insurance benefits because their entitlement period has expired; with a still threatening inflation which will not slow down as long as the government does not have the courage to reduce the interest rates to allow consumers no longer to have to pay from 30 to 40 per cent extra for the goods they purchase, with export prices which have doubled on account of the excessive tariffs set by the government, with the quotas imposed on consumer goods regulating the distribution of the production to ensure the highest possible price, with this stubbornness on the part of the government not to grant milk and food products the necessary quotas so that the producer may match his production costs rather than having to curtail his production or even destroy it, these are all the reasons why we are going through a time when our economy is very weak and the problems we are facing today so complex and difficult. They have become even more serious because of the chronic incapacity of the minister to try and cure the evil at its roots namely, the excessive interest rates which are the prime cause for this whole economic disarray. I still remember the debate I had some ten years ago before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs when the Bank Act was last revised. When it was suggested to remove any existing ceiling on the interest charged by the chartered banks, I told them at the time that Canada would face a rate of inflation higher than ever because of their mistake. That is what is happening today. The government did nothing to correct its mistake. I would even say that it made the situation worse by allowing the floating dollar. Our dollar is not the only thing that is floating now. Our entire economy is adrift while our Canadian dollar sinks and drowns. Our businessmen are sinking with it while our new Minister of Finance is fooling around on the deck of the ship claiming that everything is just fine and dandy. Except of course that our dollar is worth only 87 cents, our foreign markets are no longer competitive, the deficit of our balance of payments is enormous, our industries too poor to modernize their facilities. Other than that, no problem.
His mini-budget gives us some reason for hope. The only measure which, I think, could or would attract the attention of Canadians. In his speech the minister said
Any further stimulus should obviously be fast-acting. It should encourage consumer spending, not more spending by government...
That is what he said, but we shall see later on.
A reduction of retail sales taxes fits these requirements best.
However, everybody knows that the retail tax is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. The minister intrudes without hesitation in the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and tells them: Here I am the big federal chief. And he lays it

on thick. As elections are coming I want to give the impression that I relieve the burden of tax-payers by asking the provinces to reduce their retail sales taxes by 3 per cent. I shall repay part of it but the provinces will have to make up the difference. What a magnificient gift. Not only he intrudes in the jurisdiction of the provinces but he asks them to pay for it. Listen to what the minister says to the province:
I have offered to compensate them for a reduction of two percentage point in their retail sales tax for a period of six months.
Do you realize how long the long-term policies of the government are for; six months!
In return, I have asked them to bear the cost of either a further one percentage point for the same period, or an extension of the two-point cut for a further three-month period.
And the minister seemed surprised by the refusal of the province of Quebec faced with such an intrusion. Have we lost all the common sense of the Canadian confederation concept because of our federalist mind? Do we know at least that we have today a real Confederation made up of autonomous provinces that want to keep their autonomy? If we want Canada to survive we shall set aside our strong federal state to truly live a Confederation that commands the integrity and respect of both government levels. Why did the Federal Government not reduce the excise tax which is hidden in the price of goods so that nobody notices it?
Why not remove the tax on building materials? Why not even reduce the tax on gasoline when it is levied by both levels of government? They take their own share of the tax on gasoline, considering that we are paying today more taxes for a gallon of gasoline than for the gasoline itself. Mr. Speaker, one of these days one might suggest designing an engine which would run on taxes rather than on gasoline and that might prove to be more economical. At least the government would stop invading provincial fields of jurisdiction since they are partly or totally under federal jurisdiction. The government is even more ridiculous. It reduces the retail sales tax by 3 per cent for six to nine months after allowing the Bank of Canada to raise its interest rate to 8.5 per cent. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the consumer who wants to save 3 per cent tax during this period of six months will be forced to pay an additional 1.5 to 2 per cent in interest for five, ten, or 20 years to obtain the goods available during those six months.
That is how the government takes Canadians to the cleaners by giving them a mouse and having them pay for an elephant. And the minister goes on to say that the consumers have to be the ones who, by spending more, will stimulate the economy during the next six months. The minister sets at $1.1 billion the revenues he will draw from these operations. I doubt it very much. Even if it were true, the provinces will still have to pay $300 million and the federal government will pay only $800 million, including $350 million off the estimates of Treasury Board. The most tragic part of it all is that consumers are asked to go deeper in debt. And the example is set in
April 12, 1978

high places, Mr. Speaker, since in 1977-78 Canada was going into debt to the tune of $25 million every day, whereas in 1978-79 we will be up to a daily rate of $31 million. As we see, everything is fine, thank you. We are progressing, Mr. Speaker, we are getting closer to the day when we are totally broke.
When we know that the interest on our debt accrues at a rate of $18 million every day, it makes one wonder, Mr. Speaker. In 1978, we will pay every day $18 million in interest on our debts. In 1975, Canada's debt was $19 billion while it was $39.8 billion as of March 31, 1978. On the same day next year, it will be $51.3 billion. When will we see the end of it, Mr. Speaker?
Did you know that in this day and age debts are considered as assets? People have laughed a lot about "Caouette's buck", but "Chretien's floating buck" will make them laugh to death, because it is worth even less. With 1,045,000 unemployed, the minister has no solution other than to ask people to spend more. Increase your consumption, increase your debts, your children will pay the interest for you if they are still able to do so! The minister blames workers for not spending enough and those who have savings for not trying to invest. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I say that before the minister makes his calculations, he should meet the families who want to concentrate their savings to be able to use them for members of the family and who have a family deposit or account so that if one member of the family needs to buy a car or furniture, he can take what he needs from the family deposit and then later repay this amount, without interest charges, of course. The family deposit is part of the family and does not call for interest charges.
Many people already do this, Mr. Speaker, and I know of some people who have built a house for their son with their family deposit because it had become large enough-this can happen when 15 or 20 people make a deposit each month. This young man paid $30,000 for his house, and otherwise it would have taken him 30 years to pay for it. At the current interest rate, he would have paid $90,000 in 30 years. This young man built his house with the family credit. He will pay exactly $30,000 for it by making a monthly deposit of $200, and in seven and a half years, he will own his house. If he had gone to a finance company, he would have finished paying for his house in 30 years just before his death and he would still not be a homeowner. Indeed, this is what happened to a friend of mine who died recently. He had worked hard all his life and raised nine or ten children before dying suddenly and his wife's only consolation when I saw her was that at least his death benefits had cleared the debt on their home. This man worked all his life and he had to die to leave something to his children.
I say that we must educate people about this and if we can convince them to reduce their expenses for five years to accumulate some capital, this would kill off all the little
The Budget-Mr. C. A. Gauthier financial plans under which money is available at interest rates of 20 and 24 per cent. We would eliminate them if we could convince the population to do this. Mr. Speaker, this is social credit and it is applied very successfully in certain areas. In this way, there is no perpetual debt. In this regard, I have here a newspaper article written by Richard Johnson which states the following:
The debt of every Canadian worker amounts to $10,600.
According to the latest Statistics Canada figures, the Canadian debt on the international market has just reached $106 billion, which is an increase of 10.4 per cent over last year.
An increase of 10.4 per cent over last year is rather high, Mr. Speaker.
This simply means that every one of the ten million Canadian workers now owes $10,600 compared with $9,600 last year. A lot of good that's doing us! And then one wonders why the Canadian dollar is losing more and more value!
That amount of $106 billion represents the total debts of governments (federal, local, provincial), corporations and individuals to foreign lenders.
All we are trying to get abroad is money, because we are too cowardly to do so at home.
Canada's debt abroad has increased very fast in recent years because corporations and various governments in particular have borrowed heavily on international markets and on the New York market. Our debt has increased by more than $18 billion in the last three years alone whereas it took 15 years to reach such an amount.
The reimbursement cost for those loans in U.S. dollars, Swiss franks, German marks and Japanese yens will get increasingly higher as our dollar loses value. For example, last year Canadians paid about $9 billion in interests alone on borrowings abroad. No doubt you will be happy to learn that this interest is paid out of our taxes, our income tax and the goods we buy. The more our dollar gives down, the more we will have to pay in interest on our debt.
And so, servicing the debt costs every worker about $900.
Everyone is convinced today that shockingly high interest rates are the first cause of inflation and the ruination of our economy. What does this government suggest to fight against inflation? It increases interest rates even further. Today, a young man who wants a house will have to pay three interests to big business and one to the builder. Everyone is aware of that. Everyone understands it. The figures prove it and people recognize it. That is a fact. Everyone agrees that it is senseless, that the government should lower or freeze interest rates. Those infamous interest rates, and what's more, they are capitalized, are the ruination of our people.
The minister says that in 1974-75 he reduced the growth in expenditures by 26 per cent. That sounds good. But let us have a closer look. He reduced the growth of expenditures by 26 per cent; in 1975-76, by 18 per cent and by 10 per cent in following years. But it all depends on the rate of growth he had foreseen. Was it 20, 30 or 40 per cent? It would be interesting to know, but he does not say.
If the minister wanted to be honest with the people, he would use language they understand and tell them what the annual rate of increase in expenditures is, since, after all, they go up every year. So why speak of a decrease? Always a word to please. Why speak of a decrease when in fact it is an

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Jamieson
increase? In many services anyway. Of course, our friends must be protected, that is the civil service. All the former hon. members are there now, of course. We are well managed by a bureaucracy that has but one purpose in mind: that of doubling, if at all possible, the number of civil servants. The officials who prepared the minister's statement have thought of everything so as to make our economy look as if it was progressing whereas in fact it is seriously regressing.
A few years ago, we had one public servant for five people, today the ratio is one to three, and tomorrow it will be one to one. Meanwhile, the minister is trying to convince the public that he is controlling expenses. Expenses cannot go down if the number of public servants double. When the federal administration alone costs $2,000 per capita, we cannot be made to believe that this is normal. Mr. Speaker, as time is getting short, I would like to touch upon my last item, concerning the grants offered to research. Public servants certainly will not get any grey hair thinking about the incentives announced by the minister for research and development. Whereas there were numerous reports of the frustration encountered by university researchers because of the 20 per cent and over cut in medical research by the Canadian Medical Research Council, the minister purported to be the good Samaritan of research and development in industry, usually the larger, rather than the small or medium. While it may seem that we are giving with one hand, we are taking money away from our most productive researchers, which ends up costing millions of dollars to the taxpayers. Indeed, after the government has spent considerable sums of money on training and on the purchase of laboratory equipment, it cannot earmark the amounts necessary for the actual research once all the arsenal is there.
In that regard, Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit Party of Canada shares the view of the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies which repeatedly asked government to increase R & D funds to 2.5 per cent of the GNP by 1985, which would eliminate the unforeseen changes of the Minister of Finance, which scientists end up paying for in the wake of an election. I reiterate to the minister that he must recognize that his first budget can only disappoint the Canadian population and possibly make it reject his government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my first words today must be ones of compliment and congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who has shown the courage, under very difficult conditions, to be what he describes himself as being-a thoroughly responsible Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite have a choice this afternoon. Either they can listen to a very serious discussion on the international situation as it relates to the economy or, if they want to mix it up a little, I would be very glad to do that too. Since I understand we are a little on the short side for time, I hope they will bear with me and give me an opportunity to resist the tendency to point out in much detail some of the errors in their ways.
In any event, this afternoon I wanted to talk primarily about the context of the international situation as it relates to the Canadian economy. Before I do that, and in adding to my congratulations to the Minister of Finance, I want to speak as a Newfoundlander. In that capacity, it is with gratitude that the people of my province thank him for a reduction in the highest sale tax in the whole of Canada by a full 3 percentage points, without any payment by them for that particular gesture.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I find it rather odd that hon. members on the other side of the House would wish to dismiss a very significant reduction of that magnitude, from the highest in Canada at 11 per cent down to 8 per cent, when they were singularly silent a few weeks ago, when hon. members from Newfoundland on this side of the House were complaining that the Tory provincial government of Newfoundland had increased its sales tax by 1 percentage point. Not only have we rolled back a Tory increase of 1 per cent which occurred two weeks ago, but we have taken it down a full additional 2 percentage points.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For how long?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Having been in Newfoundland only a few days ago-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For how long?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will come to the hon. member's question in just a moment. I suspect if that gentleman were given a roomful of ponies, he would pass them up for the manure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member should listen to what is being said.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what is being spread over there.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must confess the hon. member is not contributing much to the calibre of the debate by his interruptions. He was asking how long the tax cut will last. I will get to that in a moment. However, I was in Newfoundland as recently as this past weekend, and the general level of concern about the sales tax was the biggest single item on most people's minds-that it had been escalating so steadily over the past three years. In one fell swoop, the Minister of Finance has rolled back that rate to where it was three, four or even five

April 12, 1978

years ago. That is a very profound change in the cost of living of a large number of Newfoundland people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member asked: "For how long?" It seems to me the Minister of Finance deserves commendation and not criticism for being very specific in what he wished to say about the sales tax and the duration of this particular cut. It could have been done in a way in which there would have been an implicit arrangement between himself and the provinces, but no specific declaration as to when it was going to expire. In other words, we could have played hanky-panky between the public and ourselves. At least we could have let them think that it was going to continue interminably. That would have had two effects. In the first place, it would not have been the appropriate course to take. In the second place, as the Minister of Finance said yesterday, surely it is the proper response, in terms of the requests and demands that we stimulate the economy and consumer spending, to indicate that there is a period over the next six months when consumers can take advantage of a very significant saving. The more significant it becomes, the larger the items that are purchased. Therefore, really it makes good sense to say that this measure is going to be in effect for a fixed period of time; that "here is your opportunity to take advantage of this."
Furthermore, to suggest the end of the six-month period will be the end of federal-provincial co-operation is to give the lie to the tremendous progress we have made as a result of, for example, the first ministers' conference and other discussions over the last several months. This consultative process will proceed. There is nothing to suggest, at the end of the six-month period, that there will not be other new, imaginative and creative ideas flowing from this unique process, which was introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and reinforced in these last few days by the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to say something else in reply to hon. members who say: "For how long?" Let them also ask the provincial governments: "For how long?" Let them remind themselves and the public that these are provincial sales taxes which are being reduced. There is nothing in this law, or in any other piece of legislation which is likely to be introduced, that will compel any province, including Newfoundland, to restore the 3 per cent at the end of six months or not to take any other kinds of measures.
In my judgment, as well as the judgment of many provincial ministers of Finance, the vast majority of the economists who have commented upon it, and the editorial writers who have commented upon it, this was a creative, new approach which reflected not only the wisest and best means of getting additional funds into the hands of consumers, but at the same time ensured that this government meant it and that the provincial governments meant it, when several weeks ago they said that they were prepared to embark upon a new era of co-operation.
The Budget-Mr. Jamieson
This is a prize example, and I predict that it is the first of many which will flow from it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When I rose, I indicated that I intended to talk primarily about the international situation as it affects the Canadian economy. Unfortunately, and perhaps inevitably in this kind of debate and atmosphere, there is an unreasonable tendency to assume that in some way or other Canada exists in a vacuum; that we are totally immune to the forces at play in an unprecedented way in all parts of the world; and that it is possible for us, through our own actions within Canada, to turn a situation around that is bedevilling societies and economies in every developed country of the world, and which in fact in some of those countries is actually threatening their democratic stability. One has only to look at the recent developments in many countries of the European Economic Community to see that they are in very serious difficulties, that there is a frankness in admitting this, and that in fact, as long as that situation continues, it is going to be impossible for any single country such as Canada to extract itself totally from this situation. Now, this is not to say that we cannot take measures within this parliament and the provinces to improve our position.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that not only this Minister of Finance but his predecessors also have taken a whole series of measures which, though ridiculed on the other side of the House, have, in the eyes of any objective assessment that you wish to make, produced an economic performance for Canada over these last number of years that the OECD and all the other international indicators show is better than that of all of the countries in the European Community and in the OECD membership itself. These are facts, and I ask the hon. members to look at them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Only this morning when I was in New York at the United Nations, on entirely different government business, I had an opportunity to discuss this matter with a number of people and to learn what is happening in the international community. I want to say to hon. members, and I put this to them, that despite the seriousness of our problems in Canada, if you were to measure them against those, for example, of the United States-where only yesterday the President had to make a further appeal to his countrymen to curb their inflationary tendencies and to take the measures necessary to curb rising prices in that country-we have done very well.
In the European community just last week when the nine leaders met in Copenhagen, they resolved that during the next 12 months they would have an increase of growth in their productivity of something in the order of 41/2 per cent. Taking that yardstick-a sober assessment by those leaders of what they are going to be able to achieve-surely it is not unreason-

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Jamieson
able to commend the Minister of Finance for saying that he is not only going to meet the world average in terms of growth, but also he is anticipating that our situation will be modestly better than that of the average of the countries in the OECD.
I realize that it is not as exciting to talk about the world situation as it is to hammer away at this or that matter which has a purely domestic application, but the truth of the matter is that until members of this House and the people of Canada realize it, we are not going to be able really to undertake the kind of concerted policies which have widespread support and that will bring us out of this extremely difficult world-wide situation.
I see next to me the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), and I am sure that he would confirm that the energy problems that we are facing in Canada-whether they are of tremendous magnitude or not-by world standards are much less onerous upon the Canadian consumer than those, for example, in many of the countries that I have mentioned. It is pointless for us to confuse the public or delude the public-as is often done by members opposite, and perhaps, in fairness, by all members of this House-into assuming that in a world in which there has been a quadrupling of oil prices in the last three to five years it is possible to shield consumers in this country from the effect of something which occurred in the Middle East and which is very much wrapped up in the international situation.
Surely we can pass on to the Canadian public the message that there have been fundamental changes in the world's international economic structure. Unless we have the willingness and determination in Canada, first of all, to recognize this, and then to take the steps that are necessary to counteract the problem, then not only within Canada but in the western world in general we are not going to achieve the kind of progress that all of us are anxious to have. It will not be solved by some of the measures which have been proposed by members opposite which, surely, must open them up to the accusation that they are, in fact, speaking out of both sides of their mouths at the same time.
To suggest-as has been done in this House, I understand, as recently as today-that you can introduce a $2 billion permanent tax cut and at the same time not affect the level of transfer payments, the level of service to the Canadian public, or in any other way affect the public in Canada is at the very least hypocrisy. At the very worst, it is deception of the worst possible kind, because I say it cannot be done. Hon. members by their actions daily demonstrate the inconsistency of their position. On the one hand you have this insistence or this pledge for significant across-the-board tax cuts of a permanent nature, and on the other hand they say that all of these are going to be achieved without any of the reductions that I have suggested. They say in a very general way that they would curb government spending, one after the other, day after day, week in and week out.
It would be an interesting exercise to total the value of the new demands which continue to be made by hon. members opposite on the public purse. Again, it is fair to say that you

cannot have it both ways. You either have to understand that there must be limitation, or you must be prepared to recognize the larger realities to which I have been referring. The opposition has consistently refused to do that.
What is going to happen in terms of the international community, and what hope is there if, as has been said,-not only by me but many others-that at least part of the answer, a significant part, lies outside of Canada's direct control? What are the prospects that those actions will be undertaken by the world community? I think those actions are very good. I think the prospects are very good. Canada has been recognized internationally by all countries, both developed and developing, as a country which has an excellent record in terms of economic management and the perspective that we are bringing to world problems.
If hon. members want to look askance at that kind of remark, they do not have to rely on me for the answer. They can look at the comments made by world leaders at the summit meeting which was held in London last May or June, at the OECD, and most recently, right here in Ottawa, by the vice-president of the United States when he made some most complimentary and highly deserved comments with regard to the competence and respect with which the Prime Minister of this country is held in the international community.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must say, Mr. Speaker, I have had a kind of nightmare-if 400 could describe it as such-but, certainly, it is a very disturbing prospect that comes to me when I think of the next summit meeting which is going to be held in Bonn. Just imagine the situation where the world leaders of the developed countries sit down-Giscard d'Estaing of France, James Callaghan of Britain, Mr. Fukuda of Japan, President Carter of the United States, Mr. Schmidt of West Germany, Roy Jenkins of the European community-and then they pull out the Canadian chair, and the representative speaking for this country and holding up our end of the plank is-Joe Who?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are going to lose your job.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I can say that the hon. member opposite is not going to have that kind of nightmare visited upon him. The hon. member sounds like a stick rattling around in a half empty bucket of swill.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Get on with it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are trying to have a reasonable debate on this subject.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you sit down then.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us try, at least for the few minutes that are left-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are on national television; carry on.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not even thought about it.
April 12, 1978

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. Minister has the floor for the purpose of making a speech, and I suggest we all listen to him.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What I wanted to say is that the international negotiations presently under way do provide some grounds for the hope that we will emerge from this situation starting this year. It is going to call for a tremendous amount of cooperation by all of us. Canada cannot do this on its own. If we are going to get a solution to the balance of payments problem, one has to recognize that it must be done in concert, particularly, with the European community and with Japan.
I am not sure if the statistic is familiar to all hon. members opposite or, indeed, to members on this side of the House, but it we look at Canada as an exporting country which, of course, is what we are, 87 per cent of everything that we export from Canada-everything-goes to either the United States, the European Economic Community, or Japan. That is a simple, straightforward statistic which we must recognize, and as long as there is slack in the European Community, as there is at the present time, as long as many of their basic industries are functioning at as low as 60-65 per cent capacity, as long as there are the difficulties which Japan is experiencing and, incidentally, as long as there is the confrontation between many of those countries as to how this extreme balance of payments problem is going to be resolved, then it is not going to be possible to get the kind of solutions and the kind of answers we want. I think, happily for all concerned, that this is now more in the minds of the world leaders to whom I have made reference, than at any time previously.
The decisions made in Copenhagen a few days ago may not be ones that will capture the headlines in Canada, but they are at least as important as many that are made within this country. Similarly, that summit meeting to which I referred will, as the indication in the press release said a few days ago, direct itself very clearly to the establishment of goals for increases in productivity, among other things. May I say parenthetically here, Mr. Speaker, that when members opposite talk about the low productivity in Canada, they should look at the most recent figures that have been provided, which show that not only in the last few months, or even in the last year or two, has our productivity record been better, but, in fact, over the last seven or eight years, with a couple of relatively short aberrations, there has been nothing particularly wrong with the general productivity levels in Canada in relation to those of the other developed countries.
What I am saying here is that I do not believe that it is valid to argue that in some way or other this country has lost its dynamism in terms of export markets and the like, but that in fact it is going to turn around as these markets continue to be more receptive and as their own economies improve. I do not particularly care what kind of proposal is put forward for stimulation of productivity and the like; it is not going to bite
The Budget-Mr. Jamieson
as firmly as it should in our traditional markets until cooperatively we manage to bring the whole world economy along with us.
That has been the policy of this government and it is the policy of the Minister of Finance. I think it is certainly showing results. I repeat some of the statistics I referred to earlier. With regard to any measurement you wish to apply, obviously the Canadian performance has been as good as or better than most of the other countries in the developed world.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Over what period?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would think if you took the last ten-year period there have been very few times when the Canadian performance has not been at least as good as, and in some cases better than, other countries, even including the United States.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the last two years?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member talks about the last two years. Had he been in the House earlier he would have heard me acknowledge that for the last two years there had been even more acute and special problems. If the hon. member looks at these problems objectively-which I admit is not an easy thing for him to do-he would see that in that period also, not only have we had our difficulties but they have been matched in all countries of the world, including, if he wishes to look at today's newspapers, the United States. President Carter made a very important statement yesterday with regard to the concerns in that country about what has been happening on the economic front because of a general failure-I believe these are conclusions one can draw from his remarks: everybody is to be concerned and conscious of the energy crisis and the necessity to control-not to curb or to wipe out aspirations-but to limit the demands everybody is making on the economy.
We have been doing and saying the same thing for many years. I repeat that many of the things now being proposed and introduced in other countries, and upon which consultations are taking place with Canada virtually all the time, are measures which we introduced in this country many years ago. They have come to be highly regarded, and other countries are proposing to employ them.
I believe we are going to be summoned to the other place in just a moment-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Permanently?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member I would not enjoy being in the other place-unless he is talking about being with him somewhere down below-not over there.
In all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, the message that I wanted to leave with hon. members, and I suppose it is an unreasonable expectation that it will be very receptively greeted by the other side, is that if you look at the circumstances of world economies today, you cannot fail to conclude, as we have been saying consistently on this side, that while we have problems in

April 12, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Jamieson
Canada, the Minister of Finance is seeking to diminish them. While we have those problems, we have been coming through this extremely difficult international period in a manner which is consistently better than most other societies.
I end with an invitation to hon. members to analyze the problems of the 30-odd member states of the OECD. Take each of them individually, starting with the United States and going through all the countries of Europe. Put down their record of performance and their present economic position, and then put the Canadian performance alongside. I ask hon. members under these circumstances to suppose they have the opportunity to switch Canada's problems for those of any of the other developed countries-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about Switzerland?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said the OECD. The hon. member asked what about Switzerland, but I am not sure he would even want Switzerland. I should like him to make that comparison. If we had the opportunity to switch Canada's problems with those of another country, I think the vast majority of Canadians would decide, without qualification, to take our own problems, because we continue to be one of the most fortunate countries in the world.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I think the House deserves the opportunity to thank the minister for all those detailed and concrete statistics he gave to support his broad generalizations.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on that point, I agree. I should have given the statistics. They are not very comprehensive and will be on the hon. member's desk within the hour. If any other member opposite would like to see the supporting data for anything I have said, I will be glad to provide it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, perhaps we can consider it six o'clock, because I understand there is a problem at this time-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I understand it is unfair to any person participating in the debate to expect him to commence his remarks at this moment, knowing that a message will arrive summoning us to the Senate for the purpose of Royal Assent. For the benefit of members attempting to organize their time, I think there is some merit in the suggestion of calling it six o'clock. The difficulty is that we must wait for the message to arrive.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say to the opposition that we want to collaborate. I understand it is the opposition leader who wants to speak tomorrow and we want to be sure
that he does not lose his position. We would love to see a presentation of his fiscal policies because that will provide us with a great deal of ammunition.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a verse in the Book of Revelation which says that there was silence in heaven for the space of half an hour. I do not think it would hurt us to be silent for two or three minutes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I do not think it will hurt a bit, but I do not think it is possible.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I simply rise on the point of order by the Minister of Finance (Mr.Chretien). I will convey to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) his comments. At last he is prepared to listen to some advice which has been long overdue to him in view of what he has said in his budget. To what the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has just said, I say "Amen".
